newsitem.title: POLAND: NBP keeps 1997 reserve money as operational target.
newsitem.headline: NBP keeps 1997 reserve money as operational target.

text.p: The National Bank of Poland wants to keep reserve money growth as its main operational target next year through which it could control broad money supply and inflation, the Polish central banker said on Thursday.

Hanna Gronkiewicz-Waltz told a news conference the bank set the broad money supply growth target between 27.4 and 28.6 billion zlotys next year and the reserve money growth between 5.2 and 7.5 billion zlotys.
"The central bank's main goal next year is to reduce inflation and sustain fast economic growth," Gronkiewicz-Waltz said.

"We assume that next year's economic goals will boost the demand for money in the economy in real terms by 6.8 to 7.6 percent next year, which will translate into money supply growth of bewteen 27.4 to 28.6 billion," she said.
Gronkiewicz-Waltz said such money supply growth meant net foreign currency reserves, those held by the whole banking system, would stabilise in dollar terms.

She said the bank expected credit for the economy to rise between 8.5 to 10.5 percent in real terms next year while the growth in government borrowing in the banking sector would be 10 billion zlotys.

Gronkiewicz-Waltz said the NBP's monetary policy next year will have to be restrictive because of the government's plan to leave the budget gap at 2.8 percent of gross domestic product instead of cutting it to 2.6 percent as earlier planned.
"There is a correlation between the monetary and fiscal policies (and)...since the latter has been loosened, ours will have to be more restrictive," she said.
She said in such circumstances, banks should not expect a near-term cut in obligatory reserves.
"For the time being, it (the deficit level) means that there will be no lowering (of obligatory reserves)," she said.
Gronkiewicz-Waltz also said the planned deficit level was likely to boost the government's borrowing needs, which could drive market rates up.
"Because of the higher demand for credit from the budget, market rates might rise," Gronkiewicz-Waltz said.

She said the bank assumed the zloty would be devalued, through a monthly mechanism called the crawling peg, by about nine percent next year, which would help curb inflation and induce higher productivity.

"The NBP's exchange rate policy in view of the forecasted changes in producer prices and productivity would require a devaluation of the price of the zloty against the central parity rate by about nine percent next year," she said.
"Such devaluation would support the role of the central parity rate as an anti-inflationary factor and one which forces higher productivity," she said.
